note.text: Soil conservation maintains soil’s productive and ecological functions. Cover crops and mulch reduce exposure to raindrop impact; suitable vegetation and contour measures can slow runoff. Terraces shorten and reshape slopes but need sound design and maintenance. Windbreaks can reduce wind speed near the ground. Rotations and organic inputs can support soil condition, while controlled traffic limits compaction. No method is best everywhere: waterlogging, slope stability, cost, labour and land use must be considered.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to use a labelled slope-and-cover map to prioritise erosion control and explain how a measure works. Builds on: erosion agents, runoff and soil properties. Leads to: ecosystem links and later land-use evaluation.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: The original classroom map compares invented plots under equal soil and rain. Choose the steepest bare plot for first attention rather than choosing by letter or colour alone. That is a priority exercise, not an instruction to construct works on a real farm. A vegetated contour strip can interrupt downslope flow, while a row running directly downhill can concentrate it.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Name the process, choose a measure and explain the link: cover reduces impact; a suitable barrier slows flow; roots and stable aggregates can help retain soil. Then state a limitation. Engineering, drainage and field implementation require local expertise. Pupils analyse the supplied map without cutting slopes, burning vegetation or altering a watercourse.
